Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> California Assembly Bill 1322 (AB 1322) was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom on October 13, 2023. [2] The bill, known as the California Ecosystems Protection Act of 2023, expands the state's existing moratorium on rodenticides to include the first-generation anticoagulant diphacinone. [2, 5] This legislation aims to protect wildlife, such as mountain lions, owls, and foxes, as well as children and pets, from accidental poisoning. [2, 10] The bill passed the State Assembly and various committees before being officially chaptered by the Secretary of State, becoming Chapter 836, Statutes of 2023. [3] While proponents advocate for the law to reduce unintended poisonings and protect biodiversity, some critics express concern that the restrictions could lead to rising rodent populations and the use of other, more hazardous alternatives with no antidote. [6] <2> The Tennessee Department of Agriculture (TDA) announced the first confirmed detection of the invasive spotted lanternfly (SLF) in Davidson County on September 28, 2023. This finding makes Tennessee the 16th state to report the presence of the pest since it was initially discovered in Pennsylvania in 2014. The SLF, an insect native to Asia, is considered a significant threat to a variety of crops and natural resources, with wood product businesses and fruit growers, particularly those cultivating grapes, being especially vulnerable. The insect feeds on the sap of over 70 plant species, including economically important trees like maple and black walnut, as well as its preferred host, the invasive Tree of Heaven. Infested trees can show symptoms such as wilting, dieback, and yield loss. Officials are urging the public to report sightings and destroy any spotted lanternflies or their egg masses to help control the spread. <3> The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the Department of Justice have resolved a significant and long-standing lawsuit with the Center for Biological Diversity and the Pesticide Action Network. Known as the 'megasuit,' the litigation was first filed in 2011 and alleged that the EPA violated the Endangered Species Act by failing to consult with federal wildlife agencies on the potential effects of hundreds of pesticide active ingredients on endangered and threatened species. The original lawsuit covered 382 active ingredients, which was later narrowed to 35 ingredients contained in over 1,000 pesticide products. The settlement, approved by a federal judge in San Francisco, finalizes the lawsuit and commits the EPA to a comprehensive work plan to protect endangered species. This plan involves shifting from a slow chemical-by-chemical assessment to developing broader strategies for herbicides, insecticides, rodenticides, and fungicides to mitigate risks for entire classes of pesticides. The agreement incorporates key elements from the EPA's 2022 ESA Workplan and establishes deadlines for the new strategies, representing a major development in how pesticides are regulated to protect wildlife. <4> In September 2023, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced its reception of applications for pesticide products with new active ingredients, including a plant growth regulator from UPL NA, Inc. [1, 2] This notice, covering applications received in July 2023, initiated a public comment period that was open until October 12, 2023. [1] The specific product from UPL NA, Inc. is named GAXY MUP, and its active ingredient is Ascophyllum nodosum concentrated extract, intended for use in manufacturing plant growth regulator products. [1, 2] <5> State and local authorities have established quarantines in portions of Santa Clara and Contra Costa counties in Northern California following the discovery of invasive oriental fruit flies (Bactrocera dorsalis). In Santa Clara County, the discovery of eight flies in the cities of Santa Clara and Sunnyvale led to a 112-square-mile quarantine announced in early September 2023. A subsequent discovery of seven flies in Contra Costa County near Brentwood and Oakley resulted in a 99-square-mile quarantine being declared on September 12, 2023. The oriental fruit fly is known to infest over 230 types of fruits and vegetables, posing a significant threat to California's agriculture. To eradicate the pest, the California Department of Food and Agriculture (CDFA) is implementing a treatment program using a male attractant technique, which involves applying a small amount of bait mixed with an organic pesticide to surfaces like trees and utility poles. Residents within the quarantine zones are prohibited from moving homegrown fruits and vegetables off their properties to prevent the spread of the flies. <6> In response to a 2016 Office of Inspector General report highlighting dangers associated with residential fumigations, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced its final early mitigation measures for the residential use of sulfuryl fluoride on June 29, 2023. This fumigant pesticide is used to control pests like termites, beetles, bedbugs, and rodents in residential structures. The new safety requirements are intended to increase protection for individuals and bystanders from exposure to the pesticide. The mitigation measures address findings that some air-quality testing devices were not accurately measuring when it was safe for people to re-enter a fumigated structure. The EPA's decision finalized a process that included a draft proposal and a public comment period that began in 2021. Registrants were required to submit updated product labels incorporating the new safety language for agency review. <7> In response to the detection of the invasive box tree moth (Cydalima perspectalis) in Lenawee County in November 2022, the USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) established a federal quarantine in Michigan, announced and made effective on May 30, 2023. [3, 4] This pest poses a significant threat as its caterpillars can defoliate and kill boxwood (Buxus species) plants. [8] The federal action by APHIS followed an initial intrastate quarantine set by the Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (MDARD) on April 10, 2023. [4] The initial APHIS quarantine covered all of Lenawee and Washtenaw counties, and portions of Jackson and Monroe counties, prohibiting the interstate movement of regulated items like boxwood plants and plant parts. [4] [5, 6, 8] <8> On May 17, 2023, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced it was seeking public comment on draft guidance intended to improve the efficiency of its Endangered Species Act (ESA) analyses. This initiative applies to new outdoor conventional pesticides and biopesticides, as well as existing ones undergoing registration review. The public comment period for the draft guidance officially began on May 16, 2023, and concluded on June 16, 2023. The guidance is a component of the agency's broader goals outlined in its 2022 ESA Workplan, which aims to better protect species listed as endangered or threatened from pesticide exposure. It also fulfills requirements stipulated in the Pesticide Registration Improvement Act of 2022 (PRIA 5).

The plan includes measures to reduce species' exposure to insecticides from sources like spray drift, runoff, and erosion. The Asian longhorned tick is considered a significant threat to livestock due to its ability to reproduce asexually, leading to rapid population growth, with thousands of ticks sometimes found on a single animal. These maps are designed to help create pesticide use limitation areas (PULAs), which will enable geographically specific protections for these species from pesticides. This initiative aims to improve the efficiency of the pesticide review process and increase transparency by making the data used in Endangered Species Act (ESA) assessments publicly available through interactive maps. The maps identify where listed species are likely to be found, ensuring protective measures are targeted to those specific areas, thereby reducing the impact on farmers. Developed in collaboration with the Center for Biological Diversity (CBD) and Compliance Services International (CSI), these interim maps will be finalized after a review by U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) species experts. In the two months leading up to mid-June 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed the approval of four new PFAS pesticide active ingredients. In contrast, the Mosquito Index experienced a 1 percent year-over-year decrease. <5> According to a market research report by IMARC Group, the United States pest control market, which reached a size of USD 6.1 billion in 2024, is forecast to exhibit a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 5.2% from 2025 to 2033, with projections showing it will reach USD 9.6 billion by 2033. The primary drivers for this growth include increasing urbanization, which creates ideal breeding grounds for pests, heightened public awareness of health risks like allergies and vector-borne diseases, and a growing demand for eco-friendly and sustainable pest control solutions. Other market analyses present slightly different figures; one report suggests a 5.8% CAGR from 2024 to 2033, reaching $19.2 billion, while another global report indicates a 6.3% CAGR for the pest control service market from 2024 to 2030. The public comment period on the proposal is open until July 7, 2025. <7> On May 29, 2025, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed the registration of Vadescana, a new active ingredient, to be used in products aimed at controlling Varroa mites in honeybee hives. This action is part of the EPA's ongoing efforts to provide beekeepers with new and diverse tools to combat the significant threat Varroa mites pose to the health of bee colonies and, by extension, to U.S. agriculture and food security. This action is a result of the mandatory 15-year registration review process required by the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), which assesses all aspects of a pesticide to ensure it continues to meet federal safety standards. The public comment period for this proposed rule, which was published in the Federal Register, is set to close on July 21, 2025.

The second product, Varpelgo, is a 'nature-inspired' synthetic insecticide modeled after the active ingredient Qalcova (spinosad). It targets chewing pests like caterpillars, beetles, and thrips in fruits, vegetables, row crops, and rice, and will also be available as a seed treatment to protect against wireworms. Concurrently, the EPA highlighted a new webpage dedicated to providing information on this and other biopesticides currently under review by the agency. <9> On August 13, 2025, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced its proposed registration of a new broad-spectrum fungicide, fluoxapiprolin, releasing it for public comment. The proposal covers one technical and one end-use product containing the new active ingredient, which was developed by Bayer. The fungicide is intended for use on a variety of crops, including Brassica head and stem vegetables, bulb vegetables, cucurbit vegetables, fruiting vegetables, grapes, leafy vegetables, and potatoes. It provides an alternative tool for controlling diseases such as downy mildew, late blight, and phytophthora blight and is expected to be a valuable addition to Integrated Pest Management (IPM) programs. After conducting comprehensive risk assessments, the EPA concluded that fluoxapiprolin poses no significant risks to human health or the environment when used according to label instructions and would have no adverse effects on endangered species.
